claims.text: ProductsController.List() builds a ProductDto for each row as new ProductDto(p.Id, p.Name, p.PriceVnd), read from a Product entity queried via db.Products.

DonHang.Api/Dtos.cs defines ProductDto(int Id, string Name, int PriceVnd), OrderItemDto(...), OrderDto(...), CreateOrderItemRequest(...), CreateOrderRequest(List<CreateOrderItemRequest> Items) as positional records; in a positional record each parameter becomes a public property.
claims.source_hint: examples/don-hang/DonHang.Api/Dtos.cs at tag stage-1; dotnet-docs csharp/fundamentals/types/records.md (positional parameters generate properties)

claims.text: The Product entity in DonHang.Domain has exactly the properties Id, Name, and PriceVnd, the same three ProductDto lists.
The OrderItem entity in DonHang.Domain has OrderId, ProductId, Quantity, and UnitPriceVnd; OrderItemDto omits OrderId, keeping only ProductId, Quantity, and UnitPriceVnd.

Customer in DonHang.Domain has PasswordHash (string?) alongside FullName, Email, City; null until a password is set (Entities.cs comment). It stores PasswordHasher.Hash output, a scrambled (PBKDF2) form of the password, not the password.

ASP.NET Core's default JSON options for Web API controllers set a camelCase naming policy for the response: the first word of each property name is lowercase, later words keep their capital (PriceVnd -> priceVnd). This is ASP.NET Core's web defaults, not System.Text.Json's own default behavior.
claims.source_hint: ASP.NET Core docs, Web API serialization defaults (web defaults set PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase)

claims.text: By default System.Text.Json serializes every public property of the returned type, one JSON field each, and ignores fields.
